source.title: Smaller, Weaker, Yet Better: Training LLM Reasoners via Compute-Optimal Sampling
source.authors: Hritik Bansal; Arian Hosseini; Rishabh Agarwal; Vinh Q. Tran; Mehran Kazemi

page_placements.theme: Weaker models' reasoning traces, drafts, critiques or exploration branches, filtered or rewarded with ground truth, improve a stronger model's training

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses weak-to-strong fine-tuning as a training setup and reports its performance, but does not test the specified weak-supervisor comparison or calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: The relevant experiments fine-tune Gemma2-27B on reasoning traces generated by the weaker Gemma2-9B. They compare this with fine-tuning Gemma2-27B on its own generated data, not with the weak supervisor's task performance. The paper does not report PGR. The numerical rows below capture the reported weak-data versus strong-data comparison; they do not establish that the strong student beats its weak supervisor.
record.test_reason: The study's 'weak-to-strong improvement' fine-tunes Gemma2-27B on Gemma2-9B samples filtered by gold final answers. The supervision is therefore not weak labels. It compares this against 27B trained on its own samples, never against the weak supervisor's accuracy or a strong ceiling, so no PGR can be formed. Its results bear on compute-optimal data sourcing, not on whether students exceed weak supervisors.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that at a fixed sampling budget, data from weaker, cheaper models consistently trains better reasoners than data from stronger models, across distillation, self-improvement and their W2S-I setup. They note exceptions without gold labels (Gemma MATH) and in coding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses repeated sampling of synthetic reasoning traces from a weaker LM, filters by final-answer correctness when gold answers are available, and fine-tunes using sequence-level supervised learning. It compares strong-model fine-tuning on weak-generated data against strong-model self-generated data, rather than measuring Burns et al.'s weak-to-strong PGR against a weak-supervisor baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative performance of weak- versus strong-generated data changes with task and sampling budget; with no ground-truth labels, the reported preference also depends on model pair and verification strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched sampling FLOPs, Gemma2-27B fine-tuned on gold-filtered Gemma2-9B traces beats 27B fine-tuned on its own traces on MATH (+5.8%/+4.3% relative) and GSM-8K (+1.2%/+1.5%). The effect slightly reverses without ground-truth filtering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-matched synthetic reasoning data from a weaker model can outperform a strong model's self-generated data for fine-tuning that strong model, conditional on answer verification quality.

record.problems: The paper does not report weak-supervisor performance or PGR, so its results cannot establish whether the fine-tuned strong model beats the weak supervisor. Several results are presented in figures without exact numerical values, and no uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported fine-tuning comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Other comparisons of weak- and strong-generated data for student models, coding, Gemini data, and instruction following were not extracted because they do not report the specified strong-student-versus-weak-supervisor outcome. The Functional MATH comparison is described as closely matching except at k=8, but does not give a directly usable weak-supervisor comparison or PGR.

untested.parts: No weak-supervisor accuracy, strong ceiling or PGR. Supervision is gold-filtered, not weak labels.
No auxiliary loss, supervisor ensembling or loss variants against naive weak-label training.
Model pairs and tasks vary, but PGR is never measured.
No exploitation, distribution-shift-on-PGR or error-overlap analysis. FPR of trained models is measured but is not a PGR failure test.

record.verdict_notes: The paper explicitly distinguishes its aim from Burns et al.: it seeks to enhance the strong model beyond its current level, not to recover its capabilities from weak data. An indirect comparison is possible: 9B self-trained (~39-41% MATH) vs 27B on 9B data (~45-49%), read only from figures. It is not a weak-supervisor baseline, because the generator is pretrained 9B with gold filtering, so it is not recorded as a test.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison with the weak supervisor's performance and no PGR measurement.
Does not test auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants against naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Varies models, tasks, and sampling settings, but does not measure how PGR varies or what predicts PGR.
Does not test whether students exploit supervisor-checking limits, distribution-shift effects on PGR, or error-overlap effects on PGR.
No theory establishing conditions under which a student must beat its supervisor.

relation.reason: Compares training on weak-model versus strong-model samples, principally filtered using gold answers, without a weak-supervisor performance comparison or PGR.

tranche.reason: Uses weaker-model generations to train stronger reasoners and evaluates compute-optimal data sourcing; it does not measure the catalog's weak-supervisor generalization effect.

source_check.notes: The reported percentages are relative gains over strong-model self-generated training data, not percentage-point gains or PGR. Without gold answers, Gemma results favor strong-model data under both verification strategies; Gemini results retain the weaker-data advantage.
